title: How do you secure a microservices architecture (authentication/authorization, API gateway, TLS, service mesh, secrets management, RBAC)?
shortTitle: How do you secure a microservices architecture

s1_definition.profdef: Securing a microservices architecture means applying defence in depth across multiple layers rather than trusting any single control. Authentication establishes who the caller is, typically with OAuth2 and JWT bearer tokens; authorization decides what they may do, usually with role-based access control; an API gateway terminates TLS, validates tokens, and enforces rate limits at the edge; TLS encrypts traffic in transit, including service-to-service with mutual TLS; a service mesh can enforce mTLS and policy transparently through sidecars; and secrets management keeps credentials out of code in a system like HashiCorp Vault. The guiding principle is zero trust, where no request is trusted merely because it came from inside the network.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's headquarters. At the main entrance a guard checks every visitor's ID badge, that is authentication at the API gateway. Each department door only opens for badges with the right clearance, that is role-based authorization. All the internal mail is sent in sealed, tamper-proof envelopes, that is TLS and mutual TLS between services. The master keys and vault combinations are never written on sticky notes; they live in a locked key cabinet that logs every access, that is secrets management. And nobody is trusted just because they are already inside the building; every door still checks the badge, which is zero trust.
s1_definition.oneliner: Secure microservices with defence in depth: authenticate with OAuth2 and JWT, authorize with RBAC, terminate TLS and validate tokens at the gateway, encrypt service-to-service traffic with mTLS or a mesh, keep secrets in a vault, and trust nothing merely for being inside the network.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Securing a microservices architecture means applying defence in depth across multiple layers rather than trusting any single control. Authentication establishes who the caller is, typically with OAuth2 and JWT bearer tokens; authorization decides what they may do, usually with role-based access control; an API gateway terminates TLS, validates tokens, and enforces rate limits at the edge; TLS encrypts traffic in transit, including service-to-service with mutual TLS; a service mesh can enforce mTLS and policy transparently through sidecars; and secrets management keeps credentials out of code in a system like HashiCorp Vault. The guiding principle is zero trust, where no request is trusted merely because it came from inside the network.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's headquarters. At the main entrance a guard checks every visitor's ID badge, that is authentication at the API gateway. Each department door only opens for badges with the right clearance, that is role-based authorization. All the internal mail is sent in sealed, tamper-proof envelopes, that is TLS and mutual TLS between services. The master keys and vault combinations are never written on sticky notes; they live in a locked key cabinet that logs every access, that is secrets management. And nobody is trusted just because they are already inside the building; every door still checks the badge, which is zero trust.

**One line to remember:** Secure microservices with defence in depth: authenticate with OAuth2 and JWT, authorize with RBAC, terminate TLS and validate tokens at the gateway, encrypt service-to-service traffic with mTLS or a mesh, keep secrets in a vault, and trust nothing merely for being inside the network.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with authentication, which answers who the caller is. The standard in microservices is a token-based flow using OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, where a central identity provider authenticates the user and issues a signed JWT access token. Each service then validates that token's signature and expiry without calling the identity provider on every request, which keeps services stateless and scalable. The token is a bearer credential carried in the `Authorization: Bearer` header, so protecting it with TLS and keeping its lifetime short are essential.

Authorization answers what the caller may do once authenticated. Role-based access control maps users to roles and roles to permissions, so a customer-service agent role can view accounts but a teller role can also post transactions. In Spring this is enforced with method-level annotations like `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('TELLER')")` or at the HTTP layer in the security filter chain. The roles typically ride inside the JWT as claims, so each service can authorize locally from the token without a central lookup, and for finer control you add attribute-based or policy-based checks on top.

The API gateway is the single front door and the right place to concentrate edge security. It terminates TLS so certificates are managed in one place, validates the JWT once so downstream services can trust it, applies rate limiting and throttling to blunt abuse and brute force, and routes requests to the correct service. Centralizing these concerns at the gateway means individual services do not each reimplement edge security, though they still perform their own authorization because of zero trust.

TLS protects data in transit. External traffic uses TLS so no one can read or tamper with requests between the client and the gateway. Internally, service-to-service calls should also be encrypted, and the stronger form is mutual TLS, where both the caller and the callee present certificates and verify each other, so a service only accepts calls from peers with a valid identity. This prevents an attacker who gets a foothold inside the network from freely calling internal services.

A service mesh, such as Istio or Linkerd, implements many of these concerns transparently by injecting a sidecar proxy next to each service. The mesh can enforce mutual TLS automatically for all service-to-service traffic, apply authorization policies, and provide retries, timeouts, and observability, all without changing application code. The tradeoff is operational complexity and some latency, so a mesh is most justified when you have many services and want consistent, code-free security and traffic policy.

Secrets management keeps credentials, database passwords, signing keys, and API keys out of source code and configuration files. A system like HashiCorp Vault or a cloud secrets manager stores secrets encrypted, controls who can read each secret, rotates them, and logs access, so a leaked repository never leaks live credentials. Services fetch secrets at startup or on demand with their own identity rather than embedding them.

Tying it together is zero trust: no request is trusted just because it originates inside the perimeter. Every service authenticates and authorizes every request, the network is encrypted end to end, identities are verified with mTLS, and least privilege is applied everywhere so each service and role has only the access it needs. Senior nuances include propagating a correlation identity for tracing, validating tokens' audience and issuer not just their signature, defending against token theft with short lifetimes and refresh rotation, and auditing security-relevant events centrally.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's mobile app calls several services: accounts, transfers, and statements. Without a single checkpoint, each service would reimplement login checks inconsistently, and some might forget. This is exactly the API gateway and token-validation case, where the edge authenticates once and issues a trusted token.

Problem 2 — A junior support agent should be able to view a customer's account but must never be able to post a transfer. This is exactly role-based access control, where the agent's role lacks the transfer permission.

Problem 3 — An attacker who breached one internal service tried to call the transfer service directly, bypassing the gateway. This is exactly why zero trust and mutual TLS matter: the transfer service still demands a valid token and a verified peer identity, so the internal call is rejected.

Our mini-project demonstrates these layers in a runnable way. The code defines a `Jwt` token with claims and roles, an `AuthGateway` that authenticates and issues tokens, a `RbacAuthorizer` enforcing role checks, an `AccountService` and `TransferService` that each independently authorize every call under zero trust, and a demo showing a valid customer transfer succeeding, a support agent being denied a transfer, and a forged or missing token being rejected.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three callers, a customer Rajesh, a support agent, and an attacker with a forged token, all trying to use the banking services.

Step 1: Rajesh logs in at the gateway, which verifies his credentials and issues a signed JWT carrying his subject and his CUSTOMER role. The token is the trusted credential he carries on every subsequent request.

Step 2: Rajesh calls the transfer service. The service does not trust him merely because the call arrived; under zero trust it validates the token's signature itself, confirms the CUSTOMER role includes the TRANSFER permission through the RBAC authorizer, and only then performs the transfer.

Step 3: The support agent logs in and receives a token with the SUPPORT role. When the agent views an account, the account service confirms the SUPPORT role has a view permission and allows it.

Step 4: The same agent attempts a transfer. The transfer service checks the RBAC mapping, finds that SUPPORT has no TRANSFER permission, and denies the call with a security exception. The agent's authentication was valid, but authorization correctly stopped the action.

Step 5: The attacker presents a forged token with a wrong signature. The transfer service validates the signature first, finds it does not match, and rejects the request outright before any authorization check. This shows each layer doing its job: authentication, signature validation, and role-based authorization, all enforced independently per service.

```
2026-10-24 14:49:12 INFO    Rajesh authenticated, roles=[CUSTOMER]
2026-10-24 14:49:12 INFO    TRANSFER 50000 SAV2001 → CUR3001 authorized for rajesh
2026-10-24 14:49:12 INFO    agent01 viewed account SAV2001
2026-10-24 14:49:12 SEVERE  Agent transfer DENIED: role lacks TRANSFER permission
2026-10-24 14:49:12 SEVERE  Forged token REJECTED: invalid token signature
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client (mobile)                     Attacker (forged token)
    │ login(user,password)             │ forged JWT (wrong signature)
    ▼                                  │
  ┌──────────────────────────┐        │
  │ API Gateway               │        │
  │ - TLS termination         │        │
  │ - authenticate (OAuth2)   │        │
  │ - issue signed JWT        │        │
  │ - rate limit (brute force)│        │
  └─────────────┬────────────┘         │
      Bearer JWT │                      │ bypass attempt
     ┌───────────┼──────────────────────┘
     ▼           ▼ (mTLS between services)
  AccountService    TransferService
  - validate JWT    - validate JWT signature forged → REJECT
  - RBAC VIEW       - RBAC TRANSFER?  SUPPORT  CUSTOMER
     │                 │
     ▼                 ▼
  PostgreSQL        posts transfer (ledger)

  Secrets (signing key, DB pass) ← HashiCorp Vault (never in code)
  Zero trust: EVERY service re-validates; inside-the-network ≠ trusted
```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐

  │ O: new role = new mapping entry, services unchanged           │
  │ L: any Jwt with valid signature works at any service          │
  │ D: services depend on RbacAuthorizer abstraction              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────┐ issues ┌──────────┐ validated by ┌──────────────┐
  │ AuthGateway   │───────▶│ Jwt      │─────────────▶│ TransferService│
  │ +login/+isValid│       │ subject  │              │ +transfer()    │
  └──────────────┘        │ roles    │              └──────┬────────┘
                          │ signature │                     │ uses
                          └──────────┘              ┌──────▼────────┐
                                                    │ RbacAuthorizer │
                                                    │ +hasPermission │
                                                    └──────────────┘

  ── Decision Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────
  Edge concern (TLS/rate limit/auth)? → API Gateway
  "What can they do"?                 → RBAC per service (zero trust)
  Service-to-service encryption?       → mTLS / service mesh
  Credentials/keys?                    → Vault, never in code

  ── Call Chain (transfer) ──────────────────────────────────────
  1. gateway.login → signed Jwt
  2. transferService.transfer(jwt, ...)
  3.   validator.isValid(jwt)            → signature ok?
  4.   authorizer.hasPermission(TRANSFER)→ role allows?

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Securing a microservices architecture is about defence in depth across several layers, because no single control is enough. Authentication answers who the caller is, and the standard is a token-based flow with OAuth2 and OpenID Connect, where a central identity provider authenticates the user and issues a signed JWT access token that each service validates locally by checking its signature and expiry, which keeps services stateless and scalable. Authorization answers what the caller may do, and I use role-based access control, mapping users to roles and roles to permissions, enforced with annotations like PreAuthorize or in the security filter chain, with the roles riding inside the JWT as claims so each service authorizes locally.

The API gateway is the single front door where I concentrate edge security: it terminates TLS so certificates are managed in one place, validates the JWT once, applies rate limiting to blunt abuse and brute force, and routes to the right service. TLS protects data in transit, and internally I use mutual TLS so both the caller and the callee present and verify certificates, which stops an attacker who gets a foothold inside the network from freely calling services. A service mesh like Istio can enforce that mutual TLS and authorization policy transparently through sidecars without changing application code, at the cost of some operational complexity, so I reach for it when there are many services and I want consistent, code-free security.

Secrets management keeps database passwords, signing keys, and API keys out of code and config. I store them in something like HashiCorp Vault that encrypts them, controls and logs access, and rotates them, so a leaked repository never leaks live credentials, and services fetch secrets with their own identity. Tying it all together is zero trust, where no request is trusted just because it came from inside the perimeter, so every service authenticates and authorizes every request, the network is encrypted end to end, identities are verified with mTLS, and least privilege is applied everywhere.

On my project at National Bank of India the mobile app called the accounts, transfer, and statement services, so we authenticated once at the gateway and issued a trusted JWT, but each service still validated the token and ran its own RBAC check. A support agent could view an account but was denied a transfer because the SUPPORT role simply lacked the TRANSFER permission, and when an attacker tried to call the transfer service directly with a forged token, the service rejected it on signature validation because we never trusted an internal call blindly. The lesson I always add is to validate a token's issuer and audience, not just its signature, keep token lifetimes short with refresh rotation to limit theft, and audit every authorization decision centrally.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I secure microservices with defence in depth: authenticate with OAuth2 and JWT, authorize with RBAC carried in the token, terminate TLS and validate tokens and rate-limit at the gateway, encrypt service-to-service traffic with mutual TLS or a mesh, keep every secret in a vault, and trust nothing merely because it is inside the network.

---

keyPoints: Zero-trust: verify every request, even internal
JWT propagation: gateway validates, services trust the token
mTLS: mutual TLS between services — encrypted + authenticated
RBAC/ABAC: role-based or attribute-based access control
